query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled slow‐cooling post‐heat treatment can induce coarse precipitates at the grain boundaries, producing a serrated grain boundary morphology that toughens the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy without altering its caloric phase transformation, thereby increasing its load‐bearing integrity while preserving its large caloric response under applied field and pressure.
generation.material_initial_state: The as-prepared (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits large caloric response under field and pressure but suffers from brittle behavior with a tendency to crack under load.
generation.intervention: Implement a slow-cooling post-heat treatment (from a suitable solutionizing temperature) to promote the growth of coarse precipitates along grain boundaries, thereby generating a serrated grain boundary morphology.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be applied after any necessary homogenization and prior to final cooling; the alloy’s caloric transition temperature regime (near ambient or the specific operating temperature for the caloric effect) and under the same applied field and pressure conditions used for refrigeration should be preserved.
generation.structural_mediator: Serrated grain boundaries mediated by coarse secondary precipitates at the boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coarse precipitates act as pins that force the grain boundaries to adopt an undulating, serrated morphology. This geometry distributes local stresses more uniformly, thereby reducing stress concentrations that cause crack initiation. Simultaneously, because the precipitation occurs at the boundaries and does not interfere with the bulk phase responsible for the caloric effect, the caloric response is expected to remain essentially unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in load-bearing integrity (e.g., improved tensile ductility and resistance to intergranular cracking) by an estimated relative improvement (potentially a factor of 2–3 in ductility or cracking threshold) while the caloric performance (e.g., isothermal entropy change or caloric temperature shift) remains within 10% of the baseline.
generation.baseline: The unchanged (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits excellent caloric response but suffers from crack-prone, brittle behavior that undermines its load-bearing capability.
generation.boundary: The intervention must preserve the phase responsible for the caloric response, so conditions that dramatically alter the bulk phase or caloric transition (such as overly aggressive precipitate growth or secondary phase formation interfering with the caloric mechanism) must be avoided. The test should be conducted within the operating field, pressure, and temperature regimes intended for refrigeration use.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from studies on serrated grain boundaries in HEAs (e.g., PMC9848264 sections on tensile and creep properties and PMC8840145 on microstructural evolution) supports the idea that altering grain boundary morphology improves ductility, it is uncertain how the slow-cooling process and the resulting precipitate distribution will interact with the specific phase transformation responsible for the caloric effect in (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38. The extension of these findings from conventional and eutectic HEAs to magneto- or barocaloric alloys remains to be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy specimens: (A) a control group subjected to a rapid quench after homogenization (retaining the original brittle grain boundary morphology), and (B) an experimental group subjected to a controlled slow-cooling post-heat treatment designed to induce coarse precipitates and serrated grain boundaries. After processing, conduct standardized mechanical tests (tensile and fracture toughness) along with measurements of the caloric response (e.g., isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) under identical applied field and pressure conditions.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of crack initiation and propagation (e.g., fracture strain, fracture toughness, tensile ductility)
Caloric performance metrics (e.g., isothermal entropy change, adiabatic temperature change)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/EBSD imaging to confirm serrated versus straight grain boundaries)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental group does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., at least 20% increased ductility or higher fracture toughness) without a degradation of the caloric response (performance maintained within 10% of the control), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. This work has demonstrated that a simple post heat treatment could induce SEGB in a HEA fabricated by SLM. The serrations on grain boundary in HT-samples were attributed to the blocky irregular shaped γ′ precipitates formed during the slow cooling process, and they could pin the mobile grain boundaries as well as restricting grain growth, this phenomenon is known as the Zener drag effect []. The drag force from the coarse precipitates would hinder the migration of grain boundary, while those free from the precipitates could break free around the precipitates and resulted in serrated morphology (Figure 4(c)). The inhibition of grain growth from coarse precipitates explained why HT-2 sample possessed a smaller grain size than that of HT-1 sample. The difference in tensile yield strength between HT-1 and HT-2 at 25°C and 650°C could be associated with the size of γ′ precipitates. According to Jackson – Reed model [], the strengthening contribution of γ′ precipitate could be inverse proportional to the average radius of the precipitate.
